definition: Anthrobotics is the science of developing and studying robots that are either entirely or in some way human-like.
details: The term anthrobotics was originally coined by Mark Rosheim in a paper entitled "Design of An Omnidirectional Arm" presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, May 13–18, 1990, pp. 2162–2167. Rosheim says he derived the term from "...Anthropomorphic and Robotics to distinguish the new generation of dexterous robots from its simple industrial robot forebears." The word gained wider recognition as a result of its use in the title of Rosheim's subsequent book Robot Evolution: The Development of Anthrobotics, which focused on facsimiles of human physical and psychological skills and attributes. However, a wider definition of the term anthrobotics has been proposed, in which the meaning is derived from anthropology rather than anthropomorphic. This usage includes robots that respond to input in a human-like fashion, rather than simply mimicking human actions, thus theoretically being able to respond more flexibly or to adapt to unforeseen circumstances. This expanded definition also encompasses robots that are situated in social environments with the ability to respond to those environments appropriately, such as insect robots, robotic pets, and the like. explainer.lead: Anthrobotics is the study and development of robots that are wholly or partly human-like. Its broader meaning also covers robots that respond flexibly and appropriately to people and social settings, making it relevant to both robot design and the future relationship between humans and automated systems.

tiers.eli5: Anthrobotics is about making robots a bit like people, either in how they look and move or in how they respond. It is like teaching a robotic pet not just to copy a trick, but to react sensibly when something unexpected happens.
tiers.practitioner: Anthrobotics frames robot design around human-like physical or psychological attributes, human-like responses, and appropriate behaviour in social environments. Its broader use shifts attention beyond repeating human actions towards flexible responses and adaptation to unforeseen circumstances; a pitfall is treating human-like appearance alone as sufficient.
tiers.paperLevel: Anthrobotics is formally the science of developing and studying robots that are entirely or partly human-like. Mark Rosheim coined the term in “Design of An Omnidirectional Arm,” presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation on May 13–18, 1990, combining “anthropomorphic” and “robotics”; a later, broader definition derives it from anthropology and includes flexible, socially appropriate responses. The flexible response and adaptation described by that definition are theoretical aims rather than guaranteed capabilities.

explainer.example: A robotic pet responds to input in a human-like way and adjusts its behaviour to its social surroundings. Under the expanded definition, it counts as anthrobotics even though it does not have a human-shaped body.

explainer.intuition: A robot can be human-like in its body, abilities, or behaviour, but copying human movement is only one possibility. The broader idea asks whether it can respond to input and its social surroundings in a flexible, appropriate way.
howItWorks: Choose which human-like physical or psychological attributes the robot should reproduce.
Design it to receive input rather than merely repeat fixed human actions.
Aim for responses that can flex or adapt when circumstances are unforeseen.
Place the robot in a social environment and consider whether its responses fit that environment.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects dexterous robot design with wider questions about robots living and interacting alongside people. University teaching and the Anthrobotics Cluster also use it to examine automation, intelligent systems, and what their spread means for humans.
misconceptions: Anthrobotics does not require a robot to have a fully human-shaped body.
Mimicking human actions is not the whole of the broader definition; flexible and socially appropriate responses also matter.
The expanded definition is not limited to humanoid robots and can include insect robots and robotic pets.
